monte_carlo_oprisk_capital.text: `frequency_distribution_fitting` answers "how often do loss events happen?" It takes your observed `annual_event_counts`, fits a Poisson distribution (its rate is the sample mean of those counts), and reports a dispersion ratio. A ratio far above 1 signals over-dispersion and a possible negative-binomial alternative. `monte_carlo_oprisk_capital` answers a different question: "how much capital does this loss profile imply?" It takes a Poisson rate (`frequency_lambda`) and lognormal severity settings (`severity_mu`, `severity_sigma`), then simulates many years of losses. From those it reads off the operational VaR and expected shortfall at your chosen `confidence_level`, and reports capital as OpVaR minus expected loss. The two fit together: the first one estimates the frequency input (lambda) from your data, and the second one uses that rate to build the aggregate loss distribution.

explain.text: `frequency_distribution_fitting` (Frequency Distribution Fitting) fits a Poisson distribution to the number of loss events you observed in each year, a common step in operational risk frequency modelling. You pass your yearly counts as `annual_event_counts`. It estimates the Poisson rate, lambda, as the sample mean of those counts, which is the maximum likelihood estimate. It also reports the dispersion, the variance-to-mean ratio. A value far above 1 signals over-dispersion, which may point to a negative-binomial alternative.

when.text:
Use Frequency Distribution Fitting (`frequency_distribution_fitting`) when you need to model how often operational loss events happen:

- You have observed counts of loss events per year and want a Poisson fit, where `lambda` is estimated as the sample mean of those counts.
- You want to check dispersion (variance-to-mean ratio) to see whether Poisson is reasonable. A value far above 1 signals over-dispersion and a possible negative-binomial alternative.
- You are building the frequency side of an operational risk loss model and need an input for it.
- Your data is `annual_event_counts`, one count per year.

If you need to fit the size of individual losses instead, `severity_distribution_fitting` fits a severity distribution to individual loss amounts.
